title: CLAUDE.md
text: Data frames passed likelihood methods use: - t column (ob_col): Observation times - delta column (delta_col): Event indicators - 1 = exact observation (failure) - 0 = right-censored (survived past time t) - -1 = left-censored (failed time t) Log-likelihood contributions: - Exact (δ=1): log L_i = log h(t_i) - H(t_i) - Right-censored (δ=0): log L_i = -H(t_i) - Left-censored (δ=-1): log L_i = log(1 - exp(-H(t_i)))

title: Automatic Differentiation for Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) survival models requires computing derivatives log-likelihood function. score function (gradient) needed optimization, Hessian matrix (second derivatives) needed computing standard errors confidence intervals via observed Fisher information. dfr.dist package supports three approaches computing derivatives: Pure numerical differentiation - finite differences via numDeriv Full automatic differentiation - AD computes score Hessian Hybrid approach - analytical score + AD Jacobian Hessian vignette explores approaches using Weibull distribution case study, demonstrating hybrid approach offers best combination speed precision. Note: package provides helper constructors (dfr_exponential(), dfr_weibull(), dfr_gompertz(), dfr_loglogistic()) include optimized implementations analytical cumulative hazards score functions. vignette shows build scratch understand underlying principles.

title: Automatic Differentiation for Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: femtograd package implements two AD modes dfr.dist uses different computations: Reverse-mode AD (gradients): femtograd builds computational graph value objects forward pass, calls backward() reverse topological order compute partial derivatives single backward pass. ad_gradient() uses — efficient scalar outputs (like log-likelihood) many parameters. Forward--reverse (Hessians): compute second derivatives, femtograd wraps value graph nodes dual_num objects, combining forward-mode dual numbers reverse-mode graph. ad_jacobian() uses femtograd’s dual numbers directly forward-mode pass compute Jacobian score function column--column — one pass per parameter. hybrid approach (analytical score + AD Jacobian) leverages : provide analytical gradient, ad_jacobian() differentiates using forward-mode AD obtain Hessian.

text: score function Weibull can derived analytically: ∂ℓ∂k=nk+∑ilogti−nlogσ−∑(tiσ)klog(tiσ)\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial k} = \frac{n}{k} + \sum_i \log t_i - n\log\sigma - \sum_i \left(\frac{t_i}{\sigma}\right)^k \log\left(\frac{t_i}{\sigma}\right) ∂ℓ∂σ=kσ[∑(tiσ)k−n]\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma} = \frac{k}{\sigma}\left[\sum_i \left(\frac{t_i}{\sigma}\right)^k - n\right] provide analytical score, let AD compute Jacobian (gives us Hessian): Key point: score_fn uses par[[1]] indexing (double brackets) AD compatibility. allows femtograd’s dual number objects flow Jacobian computation (uses forward-mode AD differentiate score).
code:
weibull_hybrid <- dfr_dist(     rate = function(t, par, ...) {         k <- par[[1]]         sigma <- par[[2]]         (k / sigma) * (t / sigma)^(k - 1)     },     cum_haz_rate = function(t, par, ...) {         k <- par[[1]]         sigma <- par[[2]]         (t / sigma)^k     },     score_fn = function(df, par, ...) {         k <- par[[1]]         sigma <- par[[2]]         t <- df$t         n <- length(t)          # Vectorized computation         t_over_sigma <- t / sigma         t_over_sigma_k <- t_over_sigma^k          score_k <- n/k + sum(log(t)) - n*log(sigma) -                    sum(t_over_sigma_k * log(t_over_sigma))         score_sigma <- k/sigma * (sum(t_over_sigma_k) - n)          c(score_k, score_sigma)     } )  score_hybrid <- score(weibull_hybrid) hess_hybrid <- hess_loglik(weibull_hybrid)  cat("Score (analytical):
") #> Score (analytical): print(score_hybrid(df, par = test_par)) #> [1] -10.494704   8.878147  cat("
Hessian (AD Jacobian of analytical score):
") #>  #> Hessian (AD Jacobian of analytical score): print(round(hess_hybrid(df, par = test_par), 4)) #>          [,1]     [,2] #> [1,] -73.4609  30.3410 #> [2,]  30.3410 -50.2047

Hybrid approach uses analytical score directly computes gradient without numerical integration. AD Jacobian requires 2 forward passes (one per parameter) efficient score function.

text: Used actuarial science modeling mortality. hazard rate increases exponentially: h(t;,b)=aebt,H(t;,b)=ab(ebt−1)h(t; , b) = e^{bt}, \quad H(t; , b) = \frac{}{b}(e^{bt} - 1) Score functions: ∂ℓ∂=na−1b∑(ebti−1)\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial } = \frac{n}{} - \frac{1}{b}\sum_i(e^{bt_i} - 1)∂ℓ∂b=∑iti−ab∑(tiebti1−ebti−1b)\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b} = \sum_i t_i - \frac{}{b}\sum_i \left(\frac{t_i e^{bt_i}}{1} - \frac{e^{bt_i} - 1}{b}\right)

gompertz_dist <- dfr_dist(     rate = function(t, par, ...) {         a <- par[[1]]         b <- par[[2]]         a * exp(b * t)     },     cum_haz_rate = function(t, par, ...) {         a <- par[[1]]         b <- par[[2]]         (a / b) * (exp(b * t) - 1)     },     score_fn = function(df, par, ...) {         a <- par[[1]]         b <- par[[2]]         t <- df$t         n <- length(t)         delta <- if ("delta" %in% names(df)) df$delta else rep(1, n)          exp_bt <- exp(b * t)          # Score w.r.t. a: sum(delta)/a - (1/b) * sum(exp_bt - 1)         score_a <- sum(delta) / a - sum(exp_bt - 1) / b          # Score w.r.t. b: sum(delta * t) - (a/b) * sum(t * exp_bt) + (a/b^2) * sum(exp_bt - 1)         score_b <- sum(delta * t) - (a / b) * sum(t * exp_bt) +                    (a / b^2) * sum(exp_bt - 1)          c(score_a, score_b)     } )  # Test with simulated Gompertz data # Using inverse CDF: T = (1/b) * log(1 - (b/a) * log(U)) set.seed(456) a_true <- 0.01 b_true <- 0.5 u <- runif(80) # Inverse CDF for Gompertz (when b > 0) gompertz_times <- (1/b_true) * log(1 - (b_true/a_true) * log(1-u)) gompertz_times <- gompertz_times[is.finite(gompertz_times) & gompertz_times > 0] gompertz_df <- data.frame(t = gompertz_times, delta = rep(1, length(gompertz_times)))  score_gomp <- score(gompertz_dist) hess_gomp <- hess_loglik(gompertz_dist)  cat("Gompertz distribution (a=0.01, b=0.5):
") #> Gompertz distribution (a=0.01, b=0.5): cat("  Score at true params:", round(score_gomp(gompertz_df, par = c(a_true, b_true)), 4), "

title: Creating Custom Distributions
text: simplest approach - provide hazard function: Pros: Minimal effort, works box. Cons: Cumulative hazard computed via numerical integration (slower, less accurate).
code: # Custom hazard: linear increasing failure rate # h(t) = a + b*t linear_hazard <- dfr_dist(   rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     a + b * t   },   par = c(a = 0.1, b = 0.01) )  # Everything else is computed automatically h <- hazard(linear_hazard) h(10)  # 0.1 + 0.01*10 = 0.2 #> [1] 0.2  S <- surv(linear_hazard) S(10)  # exp(-integral of hazard) #> [1] 0.2231302

title: Creating Custom Distributions
text: know closed-form integral, provide : Pros: Faster, exact cumulative hazard; enables AD gradient computation. Cons: work derive integral.
code: # H(t) = integral of (a + b*u) from 0 to t = a*t + b*t^2/2 linear_hazard_v2 <- dfr_dist(   rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     a + b * t   },   cum_haz_rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     a * t + b * t^2 / 2   },   par = c(a = 0.1, b = 0.01) )  # Now cumulative hazard uses the analytical formula H <- cum_haz(linear_hazard_v2) H(10)  # 0.1*10 + 0.01*10^2/2 = 1.5 #> [1] 1.5  # Verify survival S <- surv(linear_hazard_v2) S(10)  # exp(-1.5) ≈ 0.223 #> [1] 0.2231302 exp(-1.5) #> [1] 0.2231302

title: Creating Custom Distributions
text: fastest MLE exact Hessian, also provide score (gradient log-likelihood): Pros: Exact gradient Hessian; fastest optimization. Cons: Requires deriving score function analytically.
code: # Score derivation: # Log-likelihood for exact observation: log(h(t)) - H(t) # Log-likelihood for censored: -H(t) # # For exact: log(a + b*t) - a*t - b*t^2/2 # d/da: 1/(a+b*t) - t # d/db: t/(a+b*t) - t^2/2  linear_hazard_v3 <- dfr_dist(   rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     a + b * t   },   cum_haz_rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     a * t + b * t^2 / 2   },   score_fn = function(df, par, ...) {     a <- par[[1]]     b <- par[[2]]     t <- df$t     delta <- if ("delta" %in% names(df)) df$delta else rep(1, nrow(df))      h_vals <- a + b * t  # hazard at each observation      # d/da: sum over exact of 1/h(t) minus sum of all t     da <- sum(delta / h_vals) - sum(t)      # d/db: sum over exact of t/h(t) minus sum of all t^2/2     db <- sum(delta * t / h_vals) - sum(t^2) / 2      c(da, db)   },   par = c(a = 0.1, b = 0.01) )  # Test: score at MLE should be near zero set.seed(42) test_data <- data.frame(t = sampler(linear_hazard_v3)(50), delta = 1) solver <- fit(linear_hazard_v3) result <- solver(test_data, par = c(0.05, 0.005)) #> Warning in log(h_exact): NaNs produced #> Warning in log(h_exact): NaNs produced #> Warning in log(h_exact): NaNs produced  s <- score(linear_hazard_v3) s(test_data, par = coef(result))  # Should be ≈ (0, 0) #> [1] -0.01503346  0.38575589

title: Creating Custom Distributions
text: Cumulative hazard: H(t)=∫0t(λ+αeβu)du=λt+αβ(eβt−1)H(t) = \int_0^t (\lambda + \alpha e^{\beta u}) du = \lambda t + \frac{\alpha}{\beta}(e^{\beta t} - 1) Score function (exact observations, delta=1): ℓi=log(λ+αeβti)−λti−αβ(eβti−1)\ell_i = \log(\lambda + \alpha e^{\beta t_i}) - \lambda t_i - \frac{\alpha}{\beta}(e^{\beta t_i} - 1) Derivatives: - ∂ℓi∂λ=1h(ti)−ti\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \lambda} = \frac{1}{h(t_i)} - t_i - ∂ℓi∂α=eβtih(ti)−1β(eβti−1)\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \alpha} = \frac{e^{\beta t_i}}{h(t_i)} - \frac{1}{\beta}(e^{\beta t_i} - 1) - ∂ℓi∂β=αtieβtih(ti)+αβ2(eβti−1)−αtiβeβti\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \beta} = \frac{\alpha t_i e^{\beta t_i}}{h(t_i)} + \frac{\alpha}{\beta^2}(e^{\beta t_i} - 1) - \frac{\alpha t_i}{\beta}e^{\beta t_i}

title: Creating Custom Distributions
code: dfr_makeham <- function(lambda = NULL, alpha = NULL, beta = NULL) {   par <- if (!is.null(lambda) && !is.null(alpha) && !is.null(beta)) {     c(lambda, alpha, beta)   } else NULL    dfr_dist(     rate = function(t, par, ...) {       lambda <- par[[1]]       alpha <- par[[2]]       beta <- par[[3]]       lambda + alpha * exp(beta * t)     },     cum_haz_rate = function(t, par, ...) {       lambda <- par[[1]]       alpha <- par[[2]]       beta <- par[[3]]       lambda * t + (alpha / beta) * (exp(beta * t) - 1)     },     score_fn = function(df, par, ...) {       lambda <- par[[1]]       alpha <- par[[2]]       beta <- par[[3]]       t <- df$t       delta <- if ("delta" %in% names(df)) df$delta else rep(1, nrow(df))        exp_bt <- exp(beta * t)       h_vals <- lambda + alpha * exp_bt        # Gradient components       dlambda <- sum(delta / h_vals) - sum(t)       dalpha <- sum(delta * exp_bt / h_vals) - (1 / beta) * sum(exp_bt - 1)       dbeta <- sum(delta * alpha * t * exp_bt / h_vals) +                (alpha / beta^2) * sum(exp_bt - 1) -                (alpha / beta) * sum(t * exp_bt)        c(dlambda, dalpha, dbeta)     },     par = par   ) }

text: Model classic “bathtub” hazard three phases:
code: # Bathtub: infant mortality + useful life + wear-out # h(t) = a*exp(-b*t) + c + d*t^k dfr_bathtub <- function(a = NULL, b = NULL, c = NULL, d = NULL, k = NULL) {   par <- if (!is.null(a) && !is.null(b) && !is.null(c) &&              !is.null(d) && !is.null(k)) {     c(a, b, c, d, k)   } else NULL    dfr_dist(     rate = function(t, par, ...) {       a <- par[[1]]  # Infant mortality magnitude       b <- par[[2]]  # Infant mortality decay       c <- par[[3]]  # Baseline (useful life)       d <- par[[4]]  # Wear-out coefficient       k <- par[[5]]  # Wear-out exponent       a * exp(-b * t) + c + d * t^k     },     par = par   ) }  # Create bathtub distribution bathtub <- dfr_bathtub(a = 0.5, b = 0.3, c = 0.02, d = 0.0001, k = 2)  # Plot the bathtub curve plot(bathtub, what = "hazard", xlim = c(0, 20),      main = "Bathtub Hazard Curve", col = "darkred", lwd = 2)  # Label the three phases text(2, 0.15, "Infant\nMortality", cex = 0.8) text(8, 0.03, "Useful Life", cex = 0.8) text(17, 0.08, "Wear-out", cex = 0.8)

title: Dynamic Failure Rate Distributions
text: lifetime random variable TT, instantaneous failure rate (hazard) : h(t)=limΔt→0Pr{T≤t+Δt|T>t}Δt=f(t)S(t) h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \0} \frac{\Pr\{T \leq t + \Delta t | T > t\}}{\Delta t} = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)} cumulative hazard integrates instantaneous rate: H(t)=∫0th(u)du H(t) = \int_0^t h(u) \, du , quantities follow: Survival function: S(t)=exp(−H(t))S(t) = \exp(-H(t)) CDF: F(t)=1−S(t)F(t) = 1 - S(t) PDF: f(t)=h(t)⋅S(t)f(t) = h(t) \cdot S(t)

title: Dynamic Failure Rate Distributions
text: classic bathtub curve three phases: 1. Infant mortality: High initial failure rate decreases 2. Useful life: Low, relatively constant failure rate 3. Wear-: Increasing failure rate components age
code: # h(t) = a * exp(-b*t) + c + d * t^k # Three components: infant mortality + baseline + wear-out bathtub <- dfr_dist(   rate = function(t, par, ...) {     a <- par[1]  # infant mortality magnitude     b <- par[2]  # infant mortality decay rate     c <- par[3]  # baseline hazard (useful life)     d <- par[4]  # wear-out coefficient     k <- par[5]  # wear-out exponent     a * exp(-b * t) + c + d * t^k   },   par = c(a = 1, b = 2, c = 0.02, d = 0.001, k = 2) )  # Plot the hazard function t_seq <- seq(0.01, 15, length.out = 200) h <- hazard(bathtub) plot(t_seq, sapply(t_seq, h), type = "l",      xlab = "Time", ylab = "Hazard rate",      main = "Bathtub hazard curve")

title: Dynamic Failure Rate Distributions
text: Hazards can depend covariates modify time effect:
code: # Proportional hazards with covariate x # h(t, x) = h0(t) * exp(beta * x) # where h0(t) = Weibull baseline  ph_model <- dfr_dist(   rate = function(t, par, x = 0, ...) {     k <- par[1]     sigma <- par[2]     beta <- par[3]     baseline <- (k / sigma) * (t / sigma)^(k - 1)     baseline * exp(beta * x)   },   par = c(shape = 2, scale = 3, beta = 0.5) )  h <- hazard(ph_model)  # Hazard for different covariate values h(2, x = 0)  # Baseline #>     shape  #> 0.4444444 h(2, x = 1)  # Higher risk group #>    shape  #> 0.732765

title: Reliability Engineering Applications
text: aging system (Gompertz model), determine optimal preventive maintenance intervals.  maintenance (replacement), hazard resets initial value.
code: # System with aging characteristics system <- dfr_gompertz(a = 0.001, b = 0.002)  # Target: keep hazard below 0.05 (5% per time unit) h <- hazard(system)  # Find time when hazard reaches threshold # h(t) = a * exp(b*t) = 0.05 # t = log(0.05/a) / b threshold <- 0.05 a <- 0.001 b <- 0.002 maintenance_time <- log(threshold / a) / b  cat("Hazard threshold:", threshold, "\n") #> Hazard threshold: 0.05 cat("Maintenance interval:", round(maintenance_time, 1), "time units\n") #> Maintenance interval: 1956 time units  # Visualize plot(system, what = "hazard", xlim = c(0, 2500),      main = "Maintenance Planning", col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2) abline(h = threshold, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) abline(v = maintenance_time, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2) legend("topleft", c("Hazard", "Threshold", "Maintenance"),        col = c("darkgreen", "red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2, 2), lwd = 2)

title: Reliability Engineering Applications
text: Real products often multiple failure modes. Model additive hazards:
code: # Electronic component: constant failure rate (random defects) # Mechanical component: Weibull wear-out  dfr_competing <- function(lambda_elec = NULL, k_mech = NULL, sigma_mech = NULL) {   par <- if (!is.null(lambda_elec) && !is.null(k_mech) && !is.null(sigma_mech)) {     c(lambda_elec, k_mech, sigma_mech)   } else NULL    dfr_dist(     rate = function(t, par, ...) {       lambda <- par[[1]]       k <- par[[2]]       sigma <- par[[3]]       # Combined hazard = electronic + mechanical       lambda + (k / sigma) * (t / sigma)^(k - 1)     },     par = par   ) }  # Product with both failure modes product <- dfr_competing(lambda_elec = 0.0005, k_mech = 2.5, sigma_mech = 10000)  # Decompose contributions t_seq <- seq(1, 15000, length.out = 200) h_total <- sapply(t_seq, function(ti) hazard(product)(ti)) h_elec <- rep(0.0005, length(t_seq)) h_mech <- (2.5 / 10000) * (t_seq / 10000)^(2.5 - 1)  # Plot decomposition plot(t_seq, h_total, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 3,      xlab = "Time (hours)", ylab = "Hazard rate",      main = "Competing Failure Modes") lines(t_seq, h_elec, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2) lines(t_seq, h_mech, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend("topleft", c("Total", "Electronic", "Mechanical"),        col = c("black", "blue", "red"), lwd = c(3, 2, 2), lty = c(1, 2, 2))

title: Weibull Distribution (Power-Law Hazard) — dfr_weibull

title: Weibull Distribution (Power-Law Hazard) — dfr_weibull

title: Weibull Distribution (Power-Law Hazard) — dfr_weibull
code: # Bearing with wear-out failure (shape > 1) bearing <- dfr_weibull(shape = 2.5, scale = 50000)  # Hazard increases with time h <- hazard(bearing) h(10000)  # hazard at 10k hours #> [1] 4.472136e-06 h(40000)  # much higher at 40k hours #> [1] 3.577709e-05  # B10 life calculation Q <- inv_cdf(bearing) B10 <- Q(0.10)  # 10% failure quantile  # Fit to test data with right-censoring set.seed(123) test_data <- data.frame(   t = pmin(rweibull(100, shape = 2.5, scale = 50000), 30000),   delta = as.integer(rweibull(100, shape = 2.5, scale = 50000) <= 30000) ) solver <- fit(dfr_weibull()) result <- solver(test_data, par = c(2, 40000)) coef(result) #> [1]     6.091528 39999.995178
